title: Smooth algebraic-group orbit geometry without affine or separated hypotheses
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $G$ be a smooth group scheme of finite type over $F$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $X$ be a finite-type $F$-scheme [def-pc-scheme]. An action is a morphism $a:G\times_F X\to X$ satisfying the unit and multiplication identities [def-pc-fibre-product]. For $x\in X(F)$ let $b_x:G\to X$ be $g\mapsto gx$, and let $G_x=G\times_{X,b_x,x}\operatorname{Spec}F$ be its scheme-theoretic stabilizer. Then $G_x$ is a closed finite-type subgroup scheme of $G$. The image $O_x=b_x(|G|)$ is locally closed and has a canonical reduced induced subscheme structure: it is the reduced induced closed subscheme in any open subscheme in which its support is closed [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]. This reduced scheme is smooth and of finite type over $F$, is stable under $G$, and $b_x$ factors through a flat surjective locally finitely presented morphism $\beta_x:G\to O_x$ [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Every geometric fibre of $\beta_x$ is a translate of the corresponding base change of $G_x$. The sets $O_x(F)$ partition $X(F)$, any two supports $|O_x|$ either coincide or are disjoint, and for every algebraically closed extension $E/F$, $G(E)$ acts transitively on $O_x(E)$. For topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], $O_x$ is equidimensional and $\dim O_x=\dim G-\dim G_x$. Its closure and its boundary $\overline{O_x}\setminus O_x$ are invariant; every orbit $O_y$ contained in that boundary satisfies $\dim O_y<\dim O_x$. If $G$ is connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], $O_x$ is irreducible. No affineness or connectedness of $G$, separatedness or reducedness of $X$, or reducedness of $G_x$ is assumed.

proof.text: All schemes of finite type over $F$ are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]. Opens of them are Noetherian and quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-open-subscheme-noetherian], so their inclusions are finite type by [lem-weil-pbc-qc-open-immersion-finite-type]. Closed subschemes are finite type by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence]; finite type composes and survives base change by [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change]. Any $F$-map between the finite-type schemes here is locally of finite type by [lemma-nagata-finite-type-to-separated-target](a), which has no separatedness hypothesis. Its inverse image of each affine open is an open of a Noetherian source, hence quasi-compact, so the map is quasi-compact. Its affine coordinate maps are finitely presented by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-noetherian-finite-presentation]. Thus these maps are finite type and locally finitely presented, even when their target is not separated. The targets are quasi-separated since intersections of affine opens are opens of Noetherian schemes, hence quasi-compact. Smoothness gives geometric reducedness of $G$ by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], in particular reducedness.

source.place: Appendix A.11, A.14; Proposition 1.65, finiteness and reducedness hypotheses

proof.text: We use [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] and [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] to detect nonempty locally closed subsets by $F$-points. Indeed a locally closed subset, with its reduced induced structure, is of finite type by step 1; a closed point exists by the density statement, and its residue field is $F$. Conversely an $F$-point is closed in any $F$-scheme: in every affine neighbourhood its prime ideal is maximal because its residue field is $F$; if it had a proper specialization, an affine neighbourhood of that specialization would contain both points, a contradiction. Its morphism $\operatorname{Spec}F\to X$ is therefore a closed immersion, as is checked on affine opens by the surjection to this residue field. In particular the fibre $G_x$ is a closed subscheme of $G$ by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](b). It is finite type by step 1. On test schemes its elements are precisely $g$ with $gx=x$; the action identities show that multiplication, identity and inverse restrict, making it a subgroup scheme.

source.place: Proposition 7.5, following paragraph defining the isotropy group; Appendix A.14

proof.text: Put $b=b_x$, $S=b(|G|)$ and $Z=\overline S$. By [lem-weil-pbc-chevalley-constructible-image], $S$ is constructible. Choose an affine open $A$ meeting $S$. By [lem-wf-affine-constructible-open](2), $S\cap A$ contains a nonempty open $U$ of its closure $Z\cap A$, hence a relatively open subset of $Z$. For $g\in G(F)$ the automorphism $t_g$ of $X$, with inverse $t_{g^{-1}}$, satisfies $t_gb=bL_g$ and preserves $S$ and $Z$. The union $V=\bigcup_g t_gU$ is open in $Z$ and contained in $S$. Choose $u\in U(F)$ by step 2. The nonempty finite-type fibre of $b$ over $u$ has an $F$-point $h$, again by step 2. For every $p\in G(F)$, $b(p)=(ph^{-1})u\in V$. Thus the open $b^{-1}(V)$ contains all closed points of $G$; its closed complement is empty by step 2. Hence $S=V$, proving local closedness. This argument does not require $G$ or $Z$ to be irreducible.

Give $Z$ its reduced induced closed structure by [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme], and let $O$ be its open subscheme on $S$. Reducedness of $G$ and [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme] factor $b$ through $Z$; [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] then factors it through $O$. Write the resulting surjection as $\beta:G\to O$. It is finite type and locally finitely presented by step 1. The radical ideals defining the reduced closed structure restrict to the same radical ideals on smaller opens, so the uniqueness clause of [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme] shows that this is the reduced induced structure in every open in which $S$ is closed. Each $t_g$ restricts uniquely to an automorphism of $O$.

The Noetherian reduced $O$ has finitely many irreducible components by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components]. Delete all but one of these components and choose a nonempty affine open $D$ in the remaining open subset. This $D$ is reduced and irreducible, hence integral. Restrict $\beta$ to $D$; it is locally of finite type and quasi-compact by step 1. By [lem-sbc-generic-flatness] it is flat over a nonempty open $W\subseteq D$. For any $y\in O(F)$ the fibre of $\beta$ is nonempty finite type, so has an $F$-point. Consequently $G(F)$ is transitive on $O(F)$: if $y=\beta(h)$ and $w=\beta(p)$ then $y=(hp^{-1})w$. Choose $w\in W(F)$. The translates $t_gW$ cover all closed points and hence all of $O$ by step 2. The squares $t_g\beta=\beta L_g$ identify stalk maps over $t_gW$ with those over $W$, so these stalk maps are flat. Thus $\beta$ is flat, surjective and locally finitely presented. Only the auxiliary open $D$, not $O$, was assumed integral.

source.place: Proposition 1.65(a), generic flatness and translation argument

proof.text: The field $F$ is perfect: in characteristic $p>0$ every $a\in F$ has a root of $T^p-a$. Therefore [lem-kun-geometric-reduced-perfect] makes the reduced finite-type $O$ geometrically reduced. By [lem-pur-geometrically-reduced-dense-smooth-open] it has a dense smooth open. Its smooth locus is invariant under every $F$-isomorphism $t_g$. Choose an $F$-point in that locus; the transitivity in step 5 puts every closed point of $O$ in the smooth locus. Its closed complement is empty by step 2. Hence $O$ is smooth over $F$. This proves no smoothness assertion for $\beta$, whose stabilizer fibres can be nonreduced.

For $T=O,Z$, or $B=(Z\setminus O)_{\mathrm{red}}$, the product $G\times_F T$ is reduced by [lem-sfb-flat-geometrically-reduced-pullback]: $G/F$ is flat by [lem-pc-smooth-flat], has geometrically reduced fibres by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], and $T$ is reduced and Noetherian. The $F$-points of the product are pairs of $F$-points. Every $t_g$ preserves the supports of $O,Z,B$. First apply [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-source-factors-through-closed-subscheme] to the action into $Z$: its image is in $Z$, since the inverse image of the closed $Z$ contains every closed point by step 2. On $G\times O$ its image avoids $B$, since the inverse image of the closed $B\subset Z$ has no closed points. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] factors this action through $O$. On $G\times B$, closed-point detection and reduced-source factorization similarly give an action into $B$. Restricted action identities hold because the inclusions are monomorphisms. This proves invariance as reduced subschemes, and in particular as supports.

For every algebraically closed extension $E/F$, [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change] makes $\beta_E$ surjective. Its fibres over $O(E)$ are nonempty finite-type $E$-schemes, so [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space] and [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], applied over $E$, give lifts in $G(E)$. If $y=\beta_E(h)$, multiplication by $h$ gives an isomorphism $(G_x)_E\to(\beta_E)^{-1}(y)$; its inverse is multiplication by $h^{-1}$. These maps are inverse on every test scheme because $\beta_E(hs)=y$ exactly when $sx=x$. Thus all geometric fibres are stabilizer translates and $G(E)$ is transitive on $O(E)$. Taking $E=F$ shows $O_x(F)=G(F)x$, so these sets partition $X(F)$. If two orbit supports intersect, their intersection is a nonempty locally closed finite-type subset and has an $F$-point by step 2. The two rational orbits then agree; choosing $h\in G(F)$ with $y=hx$, the identity $b_y(g)=b_x(gh)$ gives equality of their entire supports. Otherwise the supports are disjoint.

source.place: Propositions 7.4 and 7.5, isotropy paragraph; functorial fibre-translation calculation

proof.text: The smooth $O$ is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-scheme-over-field-regular]. On any affine open, [lem-wf-smooth-components-disjoint] makes distinct irreducible components disjoint. If two global components met, their intersections with an affine neighbourhood of a meeting point would be distinct affine components: each intersection is irreducible, dense in its global component, and maximal by closing any containing irreducible subset in $O$. This contradicts the affine statement. The finitely many components of $O$ are therefore disjoint, closed and open. Every component has an $F$-point by step 2. Transitivity on these points carries any one component onto any other (an automorphism preserves maximal irreducible subsets). All have the same finite dimension $d$, finite by [lem-kun-dimension-finite-type]. Finite-union dimension gives $\dim O=d$: an irreducible closed subset of a finite union of closed sets is contained in one of them. Hence $O$ is equidimensional.

source.place: Proposition 7.4(b); Appendix A.47–A.50, equidimensionality under transitivity

proof.text: Apply [lem-sbc-flat-composite-fibre-dimension-at-point] to $G\xrightarrow{\beta}O\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ at $e\mapsto x$. Local finite type holds by step 1 and flatness by step 5, so $\dim_eG=\dim_eG_x+\dim_xO$. For $G$ and $G_x$, [lem-ag-group-identity-local-dimension] identifies identity stalk dimension with global dimension; [lem-ag-rational-point-stalk-topological-local-dimension] identifies those stalk dimensions with the topological local dimensions in the formula. By equidimensionality from step 9, [lem-sbc-equidimensional-open-local-dimension], with its open equal to $O$, gives $\dim_xO=\dim O$. All dimensions are finite by [lem-kun-dimension-finite-type], and all schemes here are nonempty. Thus $\dim G=\dim G_x+\dim O$, or $\dim O=\dim G-\dim G_x$. No regularity or reducedness of $G_x$ was used.

source.place: Appendix A.72; Stacks morphisms.tex, Tag 02JS, lemma-dimension-fibre-at-a-point-additive, equality in the flat case

proof.text: Let $C_1,\ldots,C_r$ be the components of $O$. Their closures $Z_i$ in $Z$ are exactly the irreducible components of $Z$: $Z=\bigcup_iZ_i$ since $O$ is dense and this is a finite closed union; no $Z_i$ contains another, since intersecting back with $O$ would give $C_i\subseteq C_j$. Each $C_i=Z_i\cap O$ is dense open in $Z_i$. By [lem-weil-pbc-dense-open-dimension-comparison], $\dim Z_i=\dim C_i=d$. Each closed $B\cap Z_i$ is proper. Any chain of irreducible closed subsets in it can be extended by appending $Z_i$, so its dimension is at most $d-1$. Finite-union dimension gives $\dim B<d$ when $B$ is nonempty. Every boundary orbit is contained in $B$ by step 7. Subspace monotonicity gives $\dim O_y\leq\dim B$: close a chain in the ambient space and intersect back to recover the chain, preserving strict inclusions. Hence $\dim O_y<\dim O_x$. If $B$ is empty there is no such orbit; in particular dimension zero causes no exception.

source.place: Orbit lemma 1.66 and Proposition 7.6, boundary dimension argument applied component by component

proof.text: Finally, if $G$ is connected, it is nonempty because of its identity and is regular by [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-scheme-over-field-regular]. Thus [lem-sc-regular-connected-integral] makes it integral and in particular irreducible. Its continuous surjective image $O$ is irreducible: a covering of $O$ by two closed subsets pulls back to such a covering of $G$, forcing one preimage and hence one subset to be the whole space. This establishes the last assertion while keeping all previous arguments valid for disconnected and nonaffine $G$ and nonseparated or nonreduced $X$.

source.place: Appendix A.50; continuous image of the connected smooth group, using regularity
